linkedin.body:
The number that stayed with me was 18 percent.

The European Commission asked 26,297 young people aged 13 to 18 across the 27 EU countries what they do to protect their mental wellbeing on social media. The survey ran from 30 March to 16 April 2026.

Among young people who use social media on a school day, 32 percent of those aged 13 and 14 chose talking to a parent, teacher or another adult. At 15 and 16 it was 28 percent. At 17 and 18 it was 18 percent.

That does not mean teenagers stop talking to their parents as they grow. These were three different age groups surveyed at one point, not the same children followed over time. The answer also grouped parents, teachers and other adults together. The UK was not included.

There is another part of the picture. The older group more often chose reporting harmful content or accounts and taking breaks from social media. They may be developing other ways to manage what they meet online.

Even so, the gap matters. Older teenagers in the same survey more often reported seeing AI content that was hard to recognise and unwanted sexualised content, while fewer named an adult as one of the ways they protect themselves.

It makes me think about timing. The open door is easier to build in an ordinary calm moment than when something has already gone wrong.

I build a parent tool, and one of its first lessons gives parents a simple line: if a screen ever gives you that uh oh feeling, you can always come to me. You will never be in trouble for telling me.

The research does not show that saying this changes what a teenager will do years later. It is simply a useful promise a parent can make now.

Could you say that sentence tonight, while nothing is wrong?
linkedin.firstComment:
Source: European Commission survey data analysed in a Research Square preprint published 17 November 2026:

https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11441481/v1

The strongest objection is important. This was a cross sectional survey of different age groups, not evidence that the same young people became less likely to speak to an adult over time. The response option combined a parent, teacher or another adult, and the survey did not include the UK.

instagram.caption:
STATUS: DRAFT AWAITING REVIEW

At 13 and 14, 32 percent said talking to a parent, teacher or another adult was one way they protect their wellbeing on social media.

At 17 and 18, it was 18 percent.

These were different age groups in one EU survey, not the same teenagers followed over time. The UK was not included. Older teenagers also reported other ways of coping, including reporting harmful content and taking breaks.

The useful question for parents is smaller and more practical.

Have we made it easy for our child to tell us when something online feels wrong?

facebook.caption:
STATUS: DRAFT AWAITING REVIEW

A European Commission survey asked young people who use social media on a school day what they do to protect their mental wellbeing there.

Talking to a parent, teacher or another adult was selected by 32 percent of 13 and 14 year olds, and by 18 percent of 17 and 18 year olds.

This does not show that the same children stopped talking as they grew. The groups were surveyed once, the answer included several kinds of adult, and the UK was not part of the survey. Older teenagers also more often chose reporting harmful content and taking breaks.

For families, the practical step is not to wait for a crisis. In a calm moment, we can tell a child that they can always come to us and will not be in trouble for telling us.

What words would make that promise sound natural in your family?

reveal.hooks:
CHOSEN, OVERLOOKED FINDING: The number that stayed with me was 18 percent.

COMPARISON: At 13 and 14, about a third named an adult. At 17 and 18, fewer than one in five did.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: The open door is easier to build before anyone needs it.

The comparison lost because it leads with two figures before the reader knows what was asked. The practical consequence lost because it starts with our belief rather than the evidence.

evidence.notes:
This research does not show that teenagers stop confiding in their parents as they grow. It does not separate parents from teachers or other adults. It does not establish that talking to an adult works better than reporting or taking breaks. It says nothing about UK teenagers or children under 13. It does not show that the parent promise, or Guided Childhood, changes later behaviour.
